assessmentSummary.identity: A live partner-release chase-and-capture task: wait in a declared stance, react only after a real ball drop, accelerate from a measured start mark, track and secure the ball before a declared bounce limit, decelerate inside a clear run-out, return the ball, and fully reset.
currentCardFindings: The stable legacy slug is retained, but the canonical name should specify the partner ball-drop chase-and-catch contract.

Ball Drop Reaction Drill, Reaction Ball Drop Sprint, Partner Reaction Ball Drop Sprint, and Partner Tennis Ball Drop Sprint sources describe the same base action with ball, release, distance, bounce-limit, or wording differences.
The current active generic variants do not declare release geometry, ball flight, bounce limit, capture, run-out, dose, quality gate, or stop rules and are not safely selectable.
The cone run-through/stick, required hop, second late direction cue, post-capture cut, and cue-selected gate cards have distinct ordered actions and remain separate definitions.
Five inherited YouTube links returned current oEmbed metadata, but no full-video exact-match, safety, caption, accessibility, reviewer, or approval decision has occurred.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Ball Drop Reaction Sprint is a reactive perception-action agility drill. The athlete uses clear start, plant, stop, or exit targets to rehearse visual reaction into acceleration, emphasizing low hips, clean foot placement, aligned braking, and an immediate reacceleration or stable stick depending on the drill intent.

evidence.sourceTitle: Did you see that? Dissociating advanced visual information and ball flight constrains perception and action processes during one-handed catching
claims: Ball Drop Reaction Sprint is a live partner-release task in which the athlete waits for a real ball drop, accelerates toward the object, secures it before a declared bounce limit, decelerates safely, and fully resets.

Ball type, release height and position, start stance and distance, bounce limit, and dose are exact variant or delivery fields; adding a required hop, second cue, post-capture cut, or cue-selected gate creates a different ordered action.

evidence.sourceTitle: Optimizing Agility Training in Team Sport Players—The Role of Perception-Action Coupling: A Systematic Review with Multi-Level Meta-Analysis
claims: The family combines live visual perception-action coupling, short acceleration, visual tracking, interceptive capture, and controlled deceleration.
The ball-release event must remain unpredictable enough that the athlete reacts to information rather than guessing.

evidence.sourceTitle: Sprint Acceleration Mechanics: The Major Role of Hamstrings in Horizontal Force Production
claims: Short acceleration uses coordinated hip, knee, and ankle action with meaningful posterior-chain contribution; visual tracking, reaching, and grasp add head-eye, shoulder, elbow, wrist, hand, and trunk demands.
The card records contributors and stabilizers without claiming muscle isolation.

evidence.sourceTitle: Sprint Acceleration Mechanics: The Major Role of Hamstrings in Horizontal Force Production
claims: Acceleration quality depends on effective horizontal force application and coordinated lower-limb mechanics.
A valid repetition also preserves continuous ball tracking, controlled approach speed, capture without diving or collision, and an organized run-out.

evidence.sourceTitle: Did you see that? Dissociating advanced visual information and ball flight constrains perception and action processes during one-handed catching
claims: Ball-flight information constrains gaze and hand movement, while an irregular reaction-ball bounce adds tracking and interception uncertainty.
Score only exercise complexity and physical difficulty for each exact variant, with overall equal to their maximum; athlete experience is handled through readiness and dosage.

evidence.sourceTitle: Sprint Acceleration Mechanics: The Major Role of Hamstrings in Horizontal Force Production
claims: Track high-intent starts, sprint distance, total ground contacts, braking exposures, failed captures, local posterior-chain and calf fatigue, technical change, and recovery.
Repeated sprint fatigue can change timing and mechanics, so output work stops before guessing, delayed tracking, diving, noisy braking, or speed loss.
Require a trained cue partner, declared ball, measured start distance, clear chase lane, safe capture area, and unobstructed deceleration run-out on a level nonslip surface.
The cue partner must use a visible neutral hold and release the ball without body-language or timing tells.
Short acceleration work is programmed with low repetition counts and enough recovery to preserve fast, technically controlled efforts.
Declare successful trials rather than treating every attempt as a repetition, balance release locations, and cap misses so the task does not reward reckless diving.

evidence.sourceTitle: Did you see that? Dissociating advanced visual information and ball flight constrains perception and action processes during one-handed catching
claims: Instruction must establish where to look, what constitutes the true release, the bounce limit, the allowed capture method, and the run-out before speed progresses.
Cue wait, see the release, push into the lane, track the ball, secure it without diving, and decelerate through the clear run-out.

Stop for pain, dizziness, visual disturbance, slip, fall, collision risk, unsafe reach or dive, lane intrusion, loss of braking control, repeated guessing, or a meaningful decline in acceleration or capture quality.
Do not shorten the lane, raise speed, reduce the bounce limit, or add irregular bounce until the current task remains safe and repeatable.

evidence.sourceTitle: Optimizing Agility Training in Team Sport Players—The Role of Perception-Action Coupling: A Systematic Review with Multi-Level Meta-Analysis
claims: Use the task when live perception-action coupling and first-step acceleration serve the session objective; a preplanned start does not provide the same perceptual constraint.
Place high-intent trials while the athlete is fresh and account for cumulative sprint, change-of-direction, impact, calf, Achilles, hamstring, and cognitive-decision budgets.

evidence.sourceTitle: Did you see that? Dissociating advanced visual information and ball flight constrains perception and action processes during one-handed catching
claims: The athlete needs the exact start mark, partner position, ball, release rule, bounce limit, lane, capture rule, run-out, repetitions, rest, and stop conditions before the first trial.
Nonvideo written, still-image, walkthrough, and live-demonstration alternatives remain available.

evidence.sourceTitle: Optimizing Agility Training in Team Sport Players—The Role of Perception-Action Coupling: A Systematic Review with Multi-Level Meta-Analysis
claims: The coach observes cue neutrality, false starts, release pickup, first organized step, acceleration path, gaze, capture, braking, run-out, repeatability, and fatigue.
Record successful and failed trials separately and never improve a score by making the release unsafe or ambiguous.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: Individualize task distance, speed, ball predictability, bounce limit, release height, instruction format, visual contrast, recovery, and supervision to the athlete and environment.
A rolled-ball or predictable underhand-release regression is a distinct proposed task and must not be silently substituted for the live drop contract.

evidence.sourceTitle: Alternatives to common approaches for training change of direction performance: a scoping review
claims: A point-to-gate drill, ball-drop plus late direction cue, capture-to-cut, and hop-and-go task change perception or movement actions and remain separate definitions.
Tennis-ball and reaction-ball versions remain variants only when both preserve live release, chase, secure-before-limit, controlled deceleration, and full reset.
